id_and_class.summary: Fichte grounds consciousness in the self-positing I, an original activity that is immediately present to itself before any split between subject and object. Experience arises when this activity meets a check (Anstoß) on itself, which the finite I articulates as feeling, sensation, intuition, and concept, producing a world that resists it. Full self-consciousness also requires being summoned to freedom by other rational beings.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as the I's Self-Positing Activity

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is the self-positing activity of the I, a self-relating act (Tathandlung, ‘fact-act’) that is aware of itself without making itself an object. Phenomenal experience is this activity as checked and limited.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: The body and the external world are posited by the I as the necessary correlate of its own activity, not as an independent thing-in-itself. The only I that actually exists and acts is finite, empirical, and embodied.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (self-positing is the first principle presupposed by every episode of empirical consciousness)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Every consciousness of an object already involves an implicit, pre-reflective self-relation, which Fichte holds no reflective or higher-order model can explain. Intentional object-consciousness arises when the I posits a not-I opposed to itself.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Sensory givenness is the finite I's affective encounter with its own limitation, articulated first as feeling and then as sensation. Representations felt as necessary appear objective; those felt as free appear as our own mental products. Exactly how the check yields specific sensory qualities stays obscure.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: The self-positing I (with the absolute I as an abstraction); the not-I; the check (Anstoß); finite, embodied individuals; other rational beings who summon the I to freedom.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Transcendental reflection on what must be true of subjectivity for experience to be possible, with the I's self-presence given in non-objectifying intellectual intuition.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Three principles: the I posits itself; it posits a not-I opposed to it; and it posits both as reciprocally limiting each other within consciousness. From these Fichte derives feeling, sensation, intuition of things, concepts, a spatio-temporal world, and other persons.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Pre-reflective self-awareness; object-consciousness; sensory feeling; agency and freedom; intersubjective self-consciousness.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Self-positing checked by the Anstoß. Unlimited activity could have no determinate experience, so experience of this rather than that requires the I's striving to meet resistance.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: Consciousness is ongoing activity, never a static inner field. Determinate experience is built in a sequence from feeling to sensation to intuition to concept as the I articulates its limits.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Located in finite, embodied, individual subjects, the only form in which the I actually exists.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Practical agency is central: the I strives, meets resistance, and acts, and knowledge itself depends on this practical activity.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Unity comes from the single self-positing I, a radicalized version of Kant's transcendental unity of apperception, which accompanies every representation.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Ordinary experience is a system of representations, sorted by whether they come with a feeling of necessity (the world) or a feeling of freedom (one's own thoughts).
core_claims_and_evidence: Consciousness of anything presupposes self-consciousness, and this original self-relation is an act, not a thing.
Determinate experience requires that the I's activity be checked, so the felt world is finite freedom meeting resistance.
The objective world is posited by the I, which removes Kant's unknowable thing-in-itself.
Self-conscious individuality requires a summons (Aufforderung) from another rational being.

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: The account is transcendental, not explanatory in the scientific sense: it names no neural mechanisms, psychophysical laws, or empirical criteria for consciousness. The step from the transcendental check to determinate sensory qualities is left obscure.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Interpreters dispute whether Fichte's I is the individual empirical subject or an absolute, supra-individual I. The answer decides whether his view is a theory of individual self-consciousness or a full absolute idealism.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: More thoroughgoing than Kant's idealism, since nothing outside the I's positing is retained, and distinct from Berkeley's idealism, since the individual does not invent the world at will.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: Fichte places meaning in finite freedom, practical agency, and mutual recognition among rational beings, which ground moral constraints on action.
